newsitem.title: UK: McDonnell Douglas optimistic about MD-17 cargo jet.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell Douglas optimistic about MD-17 cargo jet.

text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corporation, the U.S. aircraft manufacturer, said the cargo version of its C17 military transporter had been received with much interest from potential customers.
In a Reuter interview, MDC spokesman Richard Fuller, said a decision to offer a cargo version - designated the MD-17 - to a launch customer would be taken by the group's board soon.
The cargo aircraft is expected to be offered to the market at around U.S.$170m, said Fuller.
"We've received calls from a number of potential customers asking for briefings on the capabilities of the plane," he said.
"Originally we talked with freight forwarders because they are the ones who understand what this airplane can do and how it could be applied to their needs."

"The MD-17 is unique," he said, "it lands on short fields, it lands on austere fields and it carries bulky items that normally cannot be handled by other aircraft." The MD-17 lands on semi-prepared runways in distances of under 2,000 feet, he said.
According to Fuller, research has shown that there is "potentially a very big market for large aircraft like the MD-17".

Fuller commented: "Companies make large machines, run them to see they work and then dismantle them for shipment. Several months later, they are unpacked, reassembled and then they need experts because something does not work. There is a market to ship these large items by the MD-17 in running order straight from the factory and avoid those problems."

Commenting on other uses for the aircraft he said: "If a bottling machine breaks down in China, it is costing millions in lost revenues while it is out of action. If we fly in a replacement in the MD-17, large savings can be achieved. By surface transportation it could take months," he added.

Satellites, oil drills, heavy machines, infrastructure, helicopters, fire trucks, bulldozers and pre-assembled manufacturing plant are among the heavy items identified by MDC as suitable cargo for the four-engined MD-17 freighter.
MDC applied to the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for certification of a civil variant to the C17 aircraft in August 1996.

The MD-17 certification model has completed more than 5,000 hours of test flying. The aircraft is capable of carrying up to 170,400 pounds and it operated by a three-man crew (two pilots and a loadmaster).
It has a ferry range of 4,700 nautical miles and its four PW2040 turbofans can facilitate a 20-minute turnaround.
MDC has orders for 120 of its C17s from the U.S. Air Force, with deliveries extending to 2003.
